name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
summary: Chronic, excessive worry with somatic symptoms lasting at least 6 months. SSRIs and SNRIs (escitalopram, paroxetine, duloxetine, venlafaxine XR) carry specific GAD labeling. Buspirone and several older benzodiazepines and other anxiolytics carry broader 'anxiety disorders / symptoms of anxiety' labeling.
plainSummary: Generalized anxiety disorder means worrying too much, most days, about many things, often with tension, poor sleep, and trouble focusing. Talk therapy and daily medicines can both help.
sections: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety

approved.indication: Treatment of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in adults and pediatric patients 7 years of age and older.

population.ages: Adults and pediatric patients 7 years and older

dosing.notes: Increase to 20 mg no sooner than 1 week (adults) or 2 weeks (pediatric). Elderly and hepatic impairment: 10 mg/day. Escitalopram 15 mg capsules are labeled for GAD in adults <65 only and are not for initiation/titration.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: MAOIs (including linezolid or IV methylene blue) concurrently or within 14 days
approved.plainSummary: Escitalopram is a daily antidepressant (SSRI) approved to treat generalized anxiety in adults and children 7 and older. It usually takes a few weeks to help.

verified.note: Pediatric GAD (ages 7+) added May 2023 (Drugs@FDA efficacy supplement). Escitalopram 15 mg capsule label also checked.

approved.indication: Treatment of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in adults (Paxil immediate-release; Paxil CR is not labeled for GAD).

dosing.start: 10 mg once daily for 1 week, then 20 mg once daily
dosing.notes: Increase by 10 mg/day at weekly intervals if needed; no clear added benefit above 20 mg/day. Geriatric, severe renal or hepatic impairment: start 10 mg/day, max 40 mg/day. Taper on discontinuation.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: MAOIs (including linezolid or IV methylene blue) concurrently or within 14 days
Drugs that prolong the QTc interval and are CYP2D6 substrates (e.g., thioridazine, pimozide)
approved.plainSummary: Paroxetine is a daily antidepressant (SSRI) approved for generalized anxiety in adults. Stopping it suddenly can cause withdrawal-like symptoms.

verified.note: Label reformatted Sept 2026 (Apotex); dosing reflects current label.

approved.indication: Treatment of generalized anxiety disorder in adults and pediatric patients 7 years of age and older.

population.ages: Adults and pediatric patients 7 years and older

dosing.start: Adults: 60 mg once daily (or 30 mg once daily for 1 week); geriatric and pediatric: 30 mg once daily
dosing.notes: Increase in 30 mg increments if going above 60 mg/day; no clear added benefit above 60 mg/day. Geriatric: 30 mg for 2 weeks before increasing. 80/90/120 mg capsules are not for initiation or titration. Avoid in severe renal impairment or hepatic insufficiency (label).

formulations: Drizalma Sprinkle delayed-release capsules (can be sprinkled on applesauce or given via NG tube)
boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: MAOIs intended to treat psychiatric disorders concurrently, within 5 days of stopping duloxetine, or within 14 days of stopping the MAOI
Starting duloxetine in patients on linezolid or IV methylene blue
approved.plainSummary: Duloxetine is a daily antidepressant (SNRI) approved for generalized anxiety in adults and children 7 and older.

verified.note: Checked against Drizalma Sprinkle and a 2026 generic duloxetine delayed-release label. The Lilly Cymbalta label was not found on DailyMed on the check date (Drugs@FDA still lists Cymbalta NDA 022148 as a prescription product). Pediatric GAD (7–17) added in 2014 per Drugs@FDA supplement dates.

approved.indication: Treatment of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in adults.

dosing.start: 75 mg once daily with food (or 37.5 mg/day for 4–7 days)
dosing.notes: Increase by up to 75 mg/day at intervals of at least 4 days. Hepatic impairment: reduce dose by 50% (more in severe/cirrhosis). Renal impairment: reduce 25–50%; 50% or more in severe impairment/dialysis. Can raise blood pressure. Venlafaxine ER tablets and IR tablets are not labeled for GAD.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: MAOIs (including linezolid or IV methylene blue) concurrently or within 14 days
approved.plainSummary: Venlafaxine XR is a once-daily antidepressant (SNRI) approved for generalized anxiety in adults. It can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is checked.

approved.indication: Acute treatment of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in adults.

dosing.target: Lowest effective dose; adjust every 3–4 days
dosing.notes: Frequently reassess need for continued treatment. Taper by no more than 0.5 mg every 3 days. Geriatric, debilitated, or hepatic impairment: start 0.25 mg two or three times daily. Reduce dose with ritonavir. Xanax XR is labeled only for panic disorder.

boxedWarnings: Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
Abuse, misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death
Physical dependence and withdrawal reactions; abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to alprazolam or other benzodiazepines
Strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole), except ritonavir
Acute narrow-angle glaucoma (listed on generic ODT label)
approved.plainSummary: Alprazolam is a fast-acting benzodiazepine approved for short-term treatment of generalized anxiety in adults. It can cause dependence, and it is dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

verified.note: Current Xanax label wording is 'acute treatment of GAD'; older generic ODT labels say 'treatment of generalized anxiety disorder'.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Indicated for the management of anxiety disorders or the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety. Label notes efficacy was shown in outpatients whose diagnosis roughly corresponds to GAD.

dosing.notes: Increase by 5 mg/day every 2–3 days as needed. Take consistently with or without food. Lower dose with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Onset over weeks; not useful as needed.

contraindications: MAOIs concurrently or within 14 days; starting buspirone in patients on linezolid or IV methylene blue
approved.plainSummary: Buspirone is a non-habit-forming anxiety medicine taken every day. It takes a few weeks to work and is not used for sudden anxiety.

verified.note: BuSpar brand discontinued (Drugs@FDA). Approval year from brand history, not re-confirmed.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety or anxiety associated with depressive symptoms.

population.ages: Adults (label: safety and effectiveness not established under 12 years)

dosing.notes: Largest dose at bedtime. Elderly or debilitated: start 1–2 mg/day. Increase gradually; use a gradual taper to stop. Label wording is 'anxiety disorders'/'symptoms of anxiety' (pre-DSM-III era), not GAD specifically. Long-term (>4 months) effectiveness not systematically assessed per label.

approved.plainSummary: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine used for short-term relief of anxiety. It can cause sleepiness and dependence, and it is dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Treatment of anxiety disorders in adults who are receiving stable, evenly divided, three times daily dosing with lorazepam tablets.

dosing.start: Once daily in the morning at a dose equal to the total daily dose of lorazepam tablets
dosing.target: Same as prior total daily lorazepam dose
dosing.max: N/A (dose is converted from the stable lorazepam tablet regimen)
dosing.notes: Not for initiation. To change dose, switch back to lorazepam tablets. Capsules may be opened and sprinkled on applesauce; do not crush or chew.

boxedWarnings: Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
Abuse, misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death
Physical dependence and withdrawal reactions; abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to benzodiazepines or product ingredients
approved.plainSummary: Loreev XR is a once-a-day form of lorazepam for adults already taking lorazepam three times a day at a steady dose.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Treatment of anxiety disorders; short-term treatment of anxiety symptoms (also labeled for alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasm, and adjunctive seizure treatment).

population.ages: Adults and pediatric patients 6 months and older

dosing.start: 2–10 mg two to four times daily (adults); 2–2.5 mg once or twice daily in geriatric/debilitated patients
dosing.target: 2–10 mg two to four times daily, by severity
dosing.max: 40 mg/day (10 mg four times daily, upper end of labeled range)
dosing.notes: Pediatric (6 months and older): 1–2.5 mg three or four times daily initially, increase as tolerated. Long-term use (>4 months) not evaluated. Gradual taper to stop.

formulations: Oral solution 5 mg/5 mL and concentrate 5 mg/mL (generic)
boxedWarnings: Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
Abuse, misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death
Physical dependence and withdrawal reactions; abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal
approved.plainSummary: Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety and several other conditions. It can cause sleepiness and dependence, and it is dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

verified.note: Indication and adult dosing confirmed on the Oct 2026 Valium label. Pediatric starting dose taken from the prior Roche-format Valium label; the new label refers to section 2.2 for pediatric dosing, which was not fully reviewed. The older label also listed myasthenia gravis, severe respiratory or hepatic insufficiency, and sleep apnea as contraindications; the new label lists only hypersensitivity and acute narrow-angle glaucoma.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of symptoms of anxiety, withdrawal symptoms of acute alcoholism, and preoperative apprehension and anxiety.

population.ages: Adults and children 6 years and older

dosing.start: Mild–moderate anxiety: 5–10 mg three or four times daily
dosing.target: 5–25 mg three or four times daily, by severity
dosing.max: Severe anxiety: 20–25 mg three or four times daily (label upper range for anxiety)
dosing.notes: Geriatric/debilitated: 5 mg two to four times daily. Children 6 years and older: 5 mg two to four times daily (may increase to 10 mg two or three times daily); not recommended under 6. Label wording is 'anxiety disorders'/'symptoms of anxiety' (pre-DSM-III era), not GAD specifically. Long-term (>4 months) effectiveness not systematically assessed per label.

Physical dependence and withdrawal reactions; abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal
approved.plainSummary: Chlordiazepoxide is an older, long-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety and alcohol withdrawal. It can cause dependence and is dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

verified.note: Librium brand listed as a prescription product in Drugs@FDA.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety (also adjunctive therapy for partial seizures and symptomatic relief of acute alcohol withdrawal).

dosing.start: 15 mg/day (divided, or as a single bedtime dose); 7.5–15 mg/day in elderly or debilitated patients
dosing.notes: Adjust gradually within 15–60 mg/day. Label wording is 'anxiety disorders'/'symptoms of anxiety' (pre-DSM-III era), not GAD specifically. Long-term (>4 months) effectiveness not systematically assessed per label.

boxedWarnings: Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
Abuse, misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death

approved.plainSummary: Clorazepate is a long-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety. It can cause dependence and is dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

verified.note: Pediatric statement refers to label warning (not recommended under 9 years); no pediatric anxiety dosing given. Approval year from brand history, not re-confirmed.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety. Anxiety associated with depression is also responsive to oxazepam therapy.

population.ages: Adults (not indicated under 6 years; dosing for ages 6–12 not established)

dosing.start: Mild–moderate: 10–15 mg three or four times daily; older patients 10 mg three times daily
dosing.target: 10–30 mg three or four times daily, by severity
dosing.max: Severe anxiety: 15–30 mg three or four times daily (label upper range)
dosing.notes: Short half-life, no active metabolites (glucuronidated). Label wording is 'anxiety disorders'/'symptoms of anxiety' (pre-DSM-III era), not GAD specifically. Long-term (>4 months) effectiveness not systematically assessed per label.

boxedWarnings: Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
Abuse, misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death
Physical dependence and withdrawal reactions; abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal
approved.plainSummary: Oxazepam is a shorter-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety. It can cause dependence and is dangerous with opioids or alcohol.

verified.note: Serax brand discontinued (Drugs@FDA). Approval year from brand history, not re-confirmed.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension associated with psychoneurosis and as an adjunct in organic disease states in which anxiety is manifested.

dosing.start: Adults: 50–100 mg four times daily (label range)
dosing.notes: Children under 6: 50 mg/day in divided doses; over 6: 50–100 mg/day in divided doses. Effectiveness beyond 4 months not assessed. Sedating and anticholinergic; QT prolongation risk.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to hydroxyzine, cetirizine, or levocetirizine
approved.plainSummary: Hydroxyzine is a sedating antihistamine that is not habit-forming and can relieve anxiety and tension. It often causes drowsiness.

verified.note: Indication, dosing, and contraindications confirmed on hydroxyzine HCl tablet and pamoate capsule labels. Original approval year for this indication not confirmed. Atarax and Vistaril oral brands are listed as discontinued in Drugs@FDA.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety.

population.ages: Adults and children 6 years and older

dosing.notes: Children 6–12 years: 200–600 mg/day in 2 or 3 divided doses; not for children under 6. Habit-forming; overdose can be fatal. Long-term (>4 months) effectiveness not assessed.

contraindications: Allergic or idiosyncratic reactions to meprobamate or related compounds (e.g., carisoprodol)
approved.plainSummary: Meprobamate is an old anxiety medicine that is rarely used now because it can be habit-forming and is dangerous in overdose.

verified.note: Miltown brand discontinued (Drugs@FDA). Approval year from brand history, not re-confirmed.

approved.section: Labeled for anxiety disorders / short-term relief of anxiety
approved.indication: Effective for the short-term treatment of generalized non-psychotic anxiety; not the first drug to be used for most patients with non-psychotic anxiety. Do not exceed 6 mg/day or 12 weeks for this use (also labeled for schizophrenia).

dosing.max: 6 mg/day, for no longer than 12 weeks
dosing.notes: Higher doses or longer use for anxiety may cause persistent, possibly irreversible tardive dyskinesia (label).

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
contraindications: Comatose or greatly depressed states due to CNS depressants
Blood dyscrasias, bone marrow depression, or preexisting liver damage
approved.plainSummary: Trifluoperazine is an older antipsychotic that is labeled for short-term use at low doses for anxiety, but it is rarely used this way because of movement side effects.

verified.note: Indication and dosing confirmed. Year the non-psychotic anxiety indication was added could not be confirmed. Stelazine brand discontinued (Drugs@FDA).

offLabel.use: First-line GAD treatment (not FDA-labeled for GAD)
offLabel.notes: NICE suggests sertraline first when drug treatment is chosen for GAD. Efficacy supported in network meta-analysis. Usual SSRI cautions: early activation, GI upset, sexual dysfunction, discontinuation symptoms, boxed suicidality warning in young people.

references.label: NICE CG113: Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults (recommendations)
Slee et al. 2019, Lancet: Pharmacological treatments for GAD, network meta-analysis

offLabel.use: GAD, especially when SSRIs/SNRIs are not tolerated
offLabel.notes: Not FDA-approved for GAD in the US (approved in the EU/UK). NICE: consider if SSRIs/SNRIs not tolerated. Cautions: dizziness, sedation, weight gain, edema, misuse potential, respiratory depression with opioids or other CNS depressants, dose adjustment in renal impairment, taper to stop.

references.label: NICE CG113: Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults (recommendations)
Slee et al. 2019, Lancet: Pharmacological treatments for GAD, network meta-analysis

offLabel.notes: Effective in RCTs and network meta-analysis, but an FDA application for GAD was not approved, and NICE advises against antipsychotics for GAD in primary care. Cautions: sedation, weight gain and metabolic effects, tardive dyskinesia, boxed warnings (dementia mortality; suicidality).

references.label: Slee et al. 2019, Lancet: Pharmacological treatments for GAD, network meta-analysis
